claims.claim: Michael Dirda judges The Left Hand of Darkness to be written in a tone even more gravely austere than A Wizard of Earthsea.
claims.source: Michael Dirda, NEA Big Read Reader's Guide to A Wizard of Earthsea (NEA / Arts Midwest)
claims.quote: a tone even more gravely austere than A Wizard
claims.page: section on Le Guin's other works

claims.claim: Michael Dirda likens the fantasy or science fiction author's world-building to an anthropologist reporting on a people in as much detail as possible.
claims.source: Michael Dirda, NEA Big Read Reader's Guide to A Wizard of Earthsea (NEA / Arts Midwest)
claims.quote: just as an anthropologist reports on an indigenous people

claims.claim: The NEA Teacher's Guide describes the sentences of A Wizard of Earthsea as formal, clear and exact with the musical cadence of an oral storyteller.
claims.source: NEA Big Read Teacher's Guide to A Wizard of Earthsea (NEA / Arts Midwest)
claims.quote: formal, clear, and exact, with the musical cadence
claims.page: lesson on point of view and the narrator

claims.claim: The NEA Teacher's Guide paraphrases Le Guin as holding that heroic or high fantasy demands a slightly formal, elevated style.
claims.source: NEA Big Read Teacher's Guide to A Wizard of Earthsea (NEA / Arts Midwest)
claims.quote: a slightly formal, elevated style, commensurate with the genre's focus
claims.page: lesson on point of view and the narrator

claims.claim: The NEA Teacher's Guide says Le Guin's writing tends to be plain, strong and direct, without obvious flourish, despite occasional figurative language.
claims.source: NEA Big Read Teacher's Guide to A Wizard of Earthsea (NEA / Arts Midwest)
claims.quote: plain, strong, and direct, without obvious flourish

claims.claim: The NEA Teacher's Guide offers the novel's first sentence as the demonstration of Le Guin's plain, direct writing.
claims.source: NEA Big Read Teacher's Guide to A Wizard of Earthsea (NEA / Arts Midwest)
claims.quote: Consider the very first sentence of the novel

claims.claim: Le Guin, quoted in the NEA Teacher's Guide, says great novels offer a place, a landscape of the imagination the reader can inhabit and return to.
claims.source: NEA Big Read Teacher's Guide to A Wizard of Earthsea (NEA / Arts Midwest)
claims.quote: a landscape of the imagination which we can inhabit
claims.page: lesson on plot structure and pacing

claims.claim: Jacob Brogan asserts that in A Wizard of Earthsea Le Guin relies heavily on words with Germanic roots.
claims.source: Jacob Brogan, 'Unlearning to Write', Slate Book Review
claims.quote: relies heavily on words with Germanic roots

claims.claim: One of Le Guin's Steering the Craft exercises, quoted by Brogan, asks for a paragraph of narrative in sentences of seven or fewer words.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft, quoted by Jacob Brogan in Slate
claims.quote: in sentences of seven or fewer words

claims.claim: Le Guin, quoted by Brogan, says she finds ornate prose such as Nabokov's difficult because it is always stopping to be admired.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft, quoted by Jacob Brogan in Slate
claims.quote: difficult to get through because it's always stopping to be admired

claims.claim: Chris Mahon attributes Earthsea's succinctness to every word being carefully weighed before it goes on the page.
claims.source: Chris Mahon, '5 Things Every Fantasy Writer Can Learn from Earthsea', The Portalist
claims.quote: every word of Le Guin's is carefully weighed

claims.claim: Chris Mahon argues that Earthsea leaves a lot up to the imagination in a genre that indulges in minutiae.
claims.source: Chris Mahon, '5 Things Every Fantasy Writer Can Learn from Earthsea', The Portalist
claims.quote: Earthsea leaves a lot up to the imagination

claims.claim: Oren Ashkenazi observes that each Earthsea island the characters visit gets a few defining details, usually in terms of the local economy.
claims.source: Oren Ashkenazi, 'Building Earthsea: How Le Guin Laid a Shaky Foundation for Her World', Mythcreants
claims.quote: a few defining details, usually in terms of the local economy

claims.feature: other: prose doing the worldbuilding's work
claims.claim: Oren Ashkenazi reports that on rereading, much of what he remembered as Earthsea's worldbuilding turned out to be Le Guin's wordcraft.
claims.quote: Earthsea's worldbuilding is actually due to Le Guin's wordcraft

claims.claim: Oren Ashkenazi credits Le Guin's evocative description of a goat-charming spell with creating an impression of rarity the world's rules do not support.
claims.quote: she describes a goat-charming spell with such evocative detail

verdicts.trueWording: The Left Hand of Darkness is written in a tone even more gravely austere than A Wizard of Earthsea.
verdicts.note: Raw PDF (arts.gov, HTTP 200, pypdf text). Sentence appears verbatim in the 'other works' passage of the Reader's Guide; Acknowledgments credits 'Writer: Michael Dirda'.

verdicts.trueWording: just as an anthropologist reports on an indigenous people in as much detail as possible
verdicts.note: Raw PDF. Full sentence: '...so a science fiction or fantasy author will build up an elaborate picture of an alien culture and its inhabitants.' In the 'About the Author' page (p.5); Dirda is the credited writer.

verdicts.trueWording: The sentences are formal, clear, and exact, with the musical cadence of an oral storyteller or medieval bard.
verdicts.note: Raw PDF (Teachers-Guide-LeGuin.pdf, HTTP 200). In the narrator / point-of-view lesson (Lesson Three, FOCUS: narrator and point of view).

verdicts.trueWording: Le Guin has stressed that heroic or high fantasy demands a slightly formal, elevated style
verdicts.note: Raw PDF. Continues '...commensurate with the genre's focus on nobility of soul, heroism, and self-sacrifice.' Same point-of-view lesson; only difference is a curly vs straight apostrophe in genre's.

verdicts.trueWording: Though Le Guin occasionally uses figurative language, her writing tends to be plain, strong, and direct, without obvious flourish.
verdicts.note: Raw PDF. Lesson Five, FOCUS: Figurative Language, exactly as the claim's page field states.

verdicts.trueWording: Consider the very first sentence of the novel: 'The island of Gont...'
verdicts.note: Raw PDF. The sentence immediately follows 'plain, strong, and direct, without obvious flourish', so it is offered as the illustration of that plainness. Lesson Five.

verdicts.trueWording: Great novels offer us not only a series of events, but a place, a landscape of the imagination which we can inhabit and return to.
verdicts.note: Raw PDF. Introduced by 'Ursula K. Le Guin has written:', in Lesson Eight (FOCUS: The Plot Unfolds — plot structure and pacing).

verdicts.trueWording: she relies heavily on words with Germanic roots to convey the rawness of her windswept world
verdicts.note: Raw HTML (slate.com, HTTP 200, tags stripped locally). Third body paragraph, naming 'her fantasy novel A Wizard of Earthsea'; byline Jacob Brogan, Sept 11 2015.

verdicts.trueWording: Write a paragraph of narrative ... in sentences of seven or fewer words
verdicts.note: Raw HTML. Brogan quotes it as one of the exercises: 'goes one', in the paragraph on the book's plainspoken, practical exercises.

verdicts.trueWording: she finds such language difficult to get through because it's always stopping to be admired
verdicts.note: Raw HTML. Preceded by 'many people admire the elaborate, ornate prose of writers such as Nabokov'; in the poetry-versus-prose paragraph.

verdicts.trueWording: every word of Le Guin's is carefully weighed before being put on the page
verdicts.note: Raw HTML (theportalist.com, HTTP 200). Section 4, 'Economic prose', opening with 'Earthsea is refreshingly succinct and straightforward'; byline Chris Mahon.

verdicts.trueWording: In a genre where authors are given free rein to indulge in minutiae, Earthsea leaves a lot up to the imagination.
verdicts.note: Raw HTML. Closing sentence of section 2, 'Geography That Encourages Imagination', exactly as the page field states.

verdicts.trueWording: each island the characters visit gets at least a few defining details, usually in terms of the local economy
verdicts.note: Raw HTML (mythcreants.com, HTTP 200). Quoted string is verbatim; the claim elides the page's 'at least' before 'a few', which only weakens what the page asserts. In the 'Cool Islands' section under 'The Good'; byline Oren Ashkenazi.

verdicts.trueWording: how much of what I remembered as Earthsea's worldbuilding is actually due to Le Guin's wordcraft
verdicts.note: Raw HTML. Opens with 'When I started my reread for this article, something that constantly surprised me is...'. Placement note: this is the first paragraph of 'The Bad', mid-article, not the closing section as the page field says; that field is metadata, not a claim limb.

verdicts.trueWording: she describes a goat-charming spell with such evocative detail that it lets the reader imagine a world where even these tiny acts of sorcery are stupendous
verdicts.note: Raw HTML. The impression is of rare, treasured low-level magic, which the page rejects ('that's not the case at all') and refutes in the following 'Vague and Overpowered Magic' section. Same placement caveat as 148: it sits at the head of 'The Bad'.
